revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Refueling the Lander
revealWordProblem.text: A space-station crew has 27.6 liters of fuel to load into the lander. Each fuel cell holds exactly 3.45 liters. How many fuel cells can the crew completely fill? Make the divisor a whole number first, then divide.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: 27.6 ÷ 3.45 = 8 fuel cells. Multiply both numbers by 100 to make the divisor whole: 2760 ÷ 345 = 8. Check: 8 × 3.45 = 27.6 liters.

launch.narrative: Missed a lesson — or just want a refresher? This catch-up station reviews Lessons 1.4–1.7: 1.4 Divide Multi-Digit Numbers, 1.5 Add and Subtract Decimals, 1.6 Multiply Decimals, 1.7 Divide Decimals. Read the Big Ideas, warm up with the review problem, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 1.4–1.7
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 1.4: Subtract easy chunks of the divisor, then add up how many you took out to get the quotient. • 1.5: Line up the decimal points, add zeros so each number has the same number of decimal places, then add or subtract one column at a time. • 1.6: Multiply like whole numbers, then the product has the SAME total of decimal places as both factors combined. • 1.7: Move the decimal point the same number of places in BOTH the divisor and the dividend; the answer stays the same.

iDo.title: The Big Ideas (one per lesson)
lines: Lesson 1.4 — Divide Multi-Digit Numbers: Subtract easy chunks of the divisor, then add up how many you took out to get the quotient.
Lesson 1.5 — Add and Subtract Decimals: Line up the decimal points, add zeros so each number has the same number of decimal places, then add or subtract one column at a time.
Lesson 1.6 — Multiply Decimals: Multiply like whole numbers, then the product has the SAME total of decimal places as both factors combined.
Lesson 1.7 — Divide Decimals: Move the decimal point the same number of places in BOTH the divisor and the dividend; the answer stays the same.

weDo.title: Quick guided checks — one from each lesson
lines: From 1.4: Let's do 384 ÷ 8. What easy chunk of 8 can we take from 384? (8 × 40 = 320.)
From 1.5: Let's add 12.45 and 7.8. First, how do we write 7.8 with two decimal places? (7.80.)
From 1.6: Let's multiply 0.4 × 0.7. First multiply like whole numbers: what is 4 × 7? (28.)
From 1.7: Let's do 8.4 ÷ 2.1. How many places do we move to make 2.1 a whole number? (1 place, so 2.1 becomes 21.)

optional.stem: (Lesson 1.5) Case File: A crew member's snack receipt shows $27.60 for dried fruit and $15.45 for protein bars. What is the total on the receipt?
optional.explanation: Line up the decimal points: 27.60 + 15.45. Hundredths: 0 + 5 = 5. Tenths: 6 + 4 = 10, write 0 carry 1. Ones: 7 + 5 + 1 = 13, write 3 carry 1. Tens: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Total: $43.05.
choiceFeedback: Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?

optional.stem: (Lesson 1.6) A customer orders 3 taco baskets at $4.25 each. What is the total before tax?
optional.explanation: 3 × 425 = 1,275. The factor $4.25 has 2 decimal places, so 3 × $4.25 = $12.75.
choiceFeedback: Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
The digits are right, but where is the decimal point?
Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
hints: Estimate first: 12 × 70 = 840 and 12 × 80 = 960, so the quotient must land between 70 and 80.
Use partial quotients: subtract an easy chunk like 12 × 70 from 936, then see how many 12s fit in what's left.
Compute 936 − 840 = 96. Now ask: how many 12s make 96? Add that count to the 70 you already took out.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
hints: Size it up: 5 × 500 = 2,500, just a bit more than 2,485 — so the quotient is a little under 500.
Break 2,485 into friendly pieces that 5 divides easily, like 2,000 + 450 + 35, and divide each piece by 5.
Start with 2,000 ÷ 5 = 400. Then divide 450 by 5 and 35 by 5, and add all three partial answers together.

approaching.explanation: Line up decimals: 14.60 + 3.85. Hundredths: 0 + 5 = 5. Tenths: 6 + 8 = 14, write 4 carry 1. Ones: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Tens: 1. Answer: 18.45.
choiceFeedback: Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
hints: Notice the mismatch: 14.6 has one decimal place but 3.85 has two. Lining up the POINTS is the whole trick here.
Write 14.6 as 14.60 so both numbers show hundredths, stack the decimal points, and add column by column from the right.
Set up 14.60 + 3.85 with the points stacked. Add the hundredths (0 + 5) first, then the tenths (6 + 8) — that column carries.

approaching.explanation: Rewrite as 20.30 − 7.48. Annex a zero so both have two decimal places. Work carefully with borrowing: 20.30 − 7.48 = 12.82.
choiceFeedback: Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
hints: 20.3 stops at the tenths but 7.48 has hundredths — you can't subtract from an empty column until you annex a zero.
Rewrite the problem as 20.30 − 7.48, stack the decimal points, and subtract right to left, borrowing when the top digit is smaller.
Start at the hundredths: 0 − 8 doesn't work, so borrow from the tenths to make it 10 − 8. Keep borrowing leftward as needed.

approaching.explanation: 34 × 26 = 884. There are 2 total decimal places (1 + 1), so place the decimal to get 8.84.
choiceFeedback: The digits are right, but where is the decimal point?
Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
hints: Decimal multiplication is two jobs: multiply the digits, then place the point. Count the decimal places in BOTH factors first.
Multiply 34 × 26 as whole numbers, then give the product one decimal place for each factor — two places in total.
Compute 34 × 26 by splitting it: 34 × 20 plus 34 × 6. Then move the decimal point two places left in that product.

approaching.explanation: 7 × 15 = 105. There are 2 total decimal places (1 + 1), so place the decimal to get 1.05.
choiceFeedback: The digits are right, but where is the decimal point?
Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
hints: Both factors are close to 1, so expect an answer near 1 — a quick estimate protects you from decimal-point slips.
Multiply 7 × 15 first, ignoring the points, then count the decimal places in 0.7 and 1.5 to place the point.
Compute 7 × 15. Then count one decimal place from each factor — two total — and shift the point that many spots left.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
hints: Dividing by a decimal is awkward — notice the divisor 1.2 has one decimal place. There's a move that makes it whole.
Multiply BOTH numbers by 10: scaling dividend and divisor the same way keeps the quotient exactly the same.
Compute 14.4 × 10 = 144 and 1.2 × 10 = 12. Now solve 144 ÷ 12 — a whole-number division you already know how to do.

choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
hints: The divisor 0.6 has one decimal place — shifting both numbers one place makes the divisor a whole number.
Multiply both numbers by 10 to build an equivalent problem, then divide, keeping the decimal point in the dividend.
3.78 × 10 = 37.8 and 0.6 × 10 = 6. Now compute 37.8 ÷ 6, keeping the decimal point lined up in your answer.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.4) A warehouse has 2,184 items to pack into boxes of 14. How many boxes are needed?
choiceFeedback: Re-read the problem carefully and try again.
hints: The question asks how many groups of 14 fit into 2,184 — that phrase 'how many boxes' signals division.
Estimate to anchor yourself: 14 × 150 = 2,100 is close to 2,184. Then use partial quotients to finish.
Take out 14 × 150 = 2,100 and subtract: 2,184 − 2,100 = 84. How many 14s make 84? Add that count to 150.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 1.4) Spot the Mistake in 2,058 ÷ 14

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: Divide 2,058 ÷ 14 using partial quotients. Dividend = 2,058, divisor = 14.

onLevel.correctWork: Step 3 picks a chunk that is too big: only 98 remained, but 14 × 8 = 112 is larger than 98 — you cannot subtract more than what is left. Use the largest chunk that still fits: 14 × 7 = 98, so 98 − 98 = 0. The quotient is 100 + 40 + 7 = 147 with remainder 0. Check: 14 × 147 = 2,058, which equals the dividend.
hints: Look at Step 3: only 98 remained after Step 2. Can you really subtract 112 from 98? A negative remainder means the chunk you picked is too big.
Try the largest chunk that still fits: 14 × 7 = 98 leaves 98 − 98 = 0. So the quotient is 147 with no remainder, and 14 × 147 = 2,058.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.5) A student buys items costing $4.59, $12.75, and $3.80. What is the total cost?
onLevel.explanation: 4.59 + 12.75 + 3.80 = 21.14. Line up decimal points and add column by column.
choiceFeedback: Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
hints: Three prices, all in dollars and cents — every number already has two decimal places, so the columns line up cleanly.
Stack all three amounts with the decimal points in one column, then add the cents first, carrying as you go.
Start at the hundredths: 9 + 5 + 0 = 14 — write 4 and carry 1 into the tenths column. Keep moving left one column at a time.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 1.5) Spot the Mistake — Subtracting Without a Placeholder

workedExample.label: Set up
workedExample.work: Left 12.5 as one decimal place instead of annexing a zero

onLevel.correctWork: The student did not annex a zero, so the hundredths place had nothing to subtract from. Write 12.5 as 12.50, then line up the decimal points: 12.50 − 3.45. Hundredths: 0 − 5 → borrow → 10 − 5 = 5. Tenths: 4 − 4 = 0 (after borrowing). Ones: 2 − 3 → borrow → 12 − 3 = 9. Tens: 0 (after borrowing). The correct difference is 9.05.
hints: Check the Set up step. Does 12.5 have the same number of decimal places as 3.45?
Rewrite 12.5 as 12.50, then subtract the hundredths first. You will need to borrow to get 9.05.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.6) A car travels 55.5 miles per hour for 2.4 hours. How far does it go?
choiceFeedback: The digits are right, but where is the decimal point?
Line up the decimal points—are the place values matched?
hints: Distance = speed × time, so this is 55.5 × 2.4. Estimate 55 × 2 first so you know roughly how big the answer must be.
Multiply 555 × 24 as whole numbers, then count the decimal places: one from 55.5 plus one from 2.4.
Split it up: 555 × 24 = 555 × 20 + 555 × 4. Add those two pieces, then shift the decimal point two places left.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 1.6) Spot the Common Mistake — Placing the Decimal Point

workedExample.label: Count decimal places
workedExample.work: 1.5 has 1 decimal place and 2.4 has 1 decimal place → 2 total

workedExample.label: Place the decimal point
workedExample.work: Move the point 2 places in 360 to get 0.36

onLevel.correctWork: The whole-number product 15 × 24 = 360 and the count of 2 decimal places are both correct. The mistake is in placing the point: moving it 2 places from the right in 360 gives 3.60, not 0.36. So 1.5 × 2.4 = 3.6. An estimate of 2 × 2 = 4 confirms 3.6 is reasonable, while 0.36 is far too small.
hints: Move the point 2 places from the RIGHT end of 360. Where does it land?
360 → move 2 places from the right → 3.60 = 3.6. Estimate 2 × 2 = 4, so 3.6 is reasonable and 0.36 is wrong.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.7) A water tank holds 19.2 liters. It is poured into bottles that each hold 1.6 liters. How many bottles can be filled?
choiceFeedback: Multiply the whole numbers first, then count decimal places.
The digits look right—how many total decimal places should the product have?
hints: You're asking how many 1.6s fit into 19.2 — that's division, and the divisor 1.6 needs to become whole first.
Multiply both amounts by 10 to build an equivalent whole-number division, then divide.
19.2 × 10 = 192 and 1.6 × 10 = 16. Now divide 192 by 16 — start by taking out the chunk 16 × 10 = 160.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 1.7) Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Count how far to move
workedExample.work: 0.12 has 2 decimal places, so BOTH numbers move 2 places right. The divisor: 0.12 → 12.

workedExample.label: Move the dividend the same 2 places
workedExample.work: 9.6 only has one digit after the point, so the student moved it just 1 place: 9.6 → 96. New problem: 96 ÷ 12 = 8.

onLevel.correctWork: Both numbers must move the SAME number of places — 2, not 1. 9.6 runs out of digits after one place, so you add a placeholder zero to move the second place: 9.6 → 96 → 960. The real problem is 960 ÷ 12 = 80, so 9.6 ÷ 0.12 = 80. Estimate to confirm: 0.12 is tiny, so many of them fit in 9.6 — the quotient must be large, not 8. Check: 80 × 0.12 = 9.6. ✓
hints: The divisor moved 2 places (0.12 → 12), so the dividend has to move 2 places too — the student only moved it 1.
9.6 has no second digit to move, so add a placeholder zero: 9.6 → 960. Then 960 ÷ 12 = 80.

extending.title: (Lesson 1.4) Find Sonia's Mistake
extending.correctWork: After subtracting 80, Sonia has 16 left. 16 ÷ 16 = 1, so she needs one more partial quotient. The correct answer is 90 + 5 + 1 = 96.
hints: After Step 4, Sonia has 16 remaining. Is she really done dividing?
16 ÷ 16 = 1. She stopped too early — she needs to add that last partial quotient.

extending.title: (Lesson 1.5) Find Tasha's Mistake
extending.correctWork: Tasha did not write 15.7 as 15.70 before subtracting. With proper alignment: 15.70 − 8.36 = 7.34. She got 7.41 because she subtracted hundredths incorrectly without the placeholder zero.
hints: Look at how Tasha set up the subtraction. Does 15.7 have the same number of decimal places as 8.36?
Rewrite 15.7 as 15.70, then subtract. Hundredths: 0 − 6 requires borrowing.

extending.title: (Lesson 1.6) Find Kai's Mistake

workedExample.label: Count decimal places
workedExample.work: 2.4 has 1 decimal place, 3.15 has 2 decimal places → 2 total

extending.correctWork: Kai counted 1 + 2 = 2 decimal places, but then wrote the wrong total. The correct total is 1 + 2 = 3 decimal places. Move the decimal 3 places in 7560 to get 7.560 = 7.56.
hints: Kai counted the total decimal places wrong in Step 3. How many decimal places do 2.4 and 3.15 have together?
2.4 has 1 decimal place. 3.15 has 2 decimal places. 1 + 2 = 3 total. Move the decimal 3 places: 7.560.

extending.title: (Lesson 1.7) Find Derek's Mistake
extending.correctWork: Derek only multiplied by 10, but the divisor 0.45 has two decimal places. He should multiply both numbers by 100: 720 ÷ 45 = 16. He got the right answer by luck this time, but his method is unreliable because the divisor is still a decimal (4.5).
hints: How many decimal places does 0.45 have? Did Derek multiply by enough to make it a whole number?
0.45 has two decimal places, so multiply both by 100, not 10. 0.45 × 100 = 45 and 7.2 × 100 = 720.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Divide Decimals is moving the decimal point in the divisor but forgetting to move it the same number of places in the dividend. For example, in 6.4 ÷ 0.8 a student changes 0.8 to 8 but leaves the dividend as 6.4, then divides 6.4 ÷ 8 = 0.8 instead of moving both points to get 64 ÷ 8 = 8. A second version of this mistake happens when the divisor has two decimal places, like 0.12: students move both points only 1 place instead of 2, turning 9.6 ÷ 0.12 into 96 ÷ 1.2 instead of the correct 960 ÷ 12. Count the divisor's decimal places first, then move BOTH points that same number of places.
